title: Registration and device-enrollment data can reveal household identity and setup details
description: The flow carries account-registration details and enrollment information for cameras/sensors from the homeowner to the Home Hub. These data can identify the homeowner or household and disclose the presence, type, and number of devices in the home, enabling inference about the occupants and security setup if exposed to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment payload includes personal identifiers (e.g., email, account name) and device metadata such as device IDs, model/type, room/location labels, or similar setup information.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types for ExternalEntity->Process flows but not the detailed I-subtree nodes.

title: Enrollment payload enables profiling of the household and living environment
description: Combining account-registration data with enrolled camera/sensor metadata allows the Home Hub to derive privacy-sensitive characteristics of the household, such as home size, occupancy patterns, security posture, and possibly vulnerable areas being monitored. Even if each field seems benign, the aggregate can disclose sensitive facts about the residents.
assumptions: Assumes the hub or connected services can correlate multiple enrolled devices and associated labels/locations during onboarding.
uncertainty_note: Detailed D-subtree node chosen by best judgement; the supplied mapping context does not include specific threat-tree node ids.

title: Users may be unaware of the full extent of personal and device data collected during onboarding
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may not understand which personal data, device identifiers, configuration details, and inferred household characteristics are collected and processed by the Home Hub. This creates a privacy threat if the collection is not transparent at the point of data entry.
assumptions: Assumes onboarding UX does not clearly explain all collected fields, downstream uses, retention, or sharing.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the actual onboarding notices and UX; included because this flow is a common point where unawareness arises.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect more data than necessary or without valid consent/legal basis
description: The onboarding flow may request or transmit personal details and detailed device metadata beyond what is strictly necessary to create an account and enroll devices, or may do so before obtaining valid consent or establishing another lawful basis. This creates a non-compliance risk tied directly to the data flow.
assumptions: Assumes at least some fields in registration/enrollment are optional or not strictly necessary, or that consent/legal notices are incomplete at collection time.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine risk pattern for onboarding flows, but actual applicability depends on the implemented data-minimization and consent/legal-basis design.

title: Temporary access code can reveal guest identity or visit pattern
description: The Home Hub receives a temporary access code from the guest. If the code is unique per guest or per visit, the hub can infer or record which guest is attempting entry and when, enabling identification of a person or household visitor pattern from this flow.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are uniquely assigned to a guest, booking, or time window rather than being a shared generic code.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context did not include a specific Identifiability node citation.

title: Entry code disclosure in transit or at input interface
description: The temporary access code is privacy-sensitive authentication data. If the code is exposed while being entered, transmitted from the keypad/UI to processing logic, or logged by the Home Hub, an observer or unauthorized party could learn the guest's access credential and associated entry event.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub includes a user interface and internal communication or logging path where the code could be exposed.
uncertainty_note: Threat is grounded in disclosure of the code and associated access event on this flow; exact threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Guest may be unaware that code entry is personal data being collected
description: When entering the temporary access code, the guest may not realize the Home Hub is collecting data about their access attempt, such as the code used, timestamp, success/failure, and linkage to a guest stay. This creates unawareness about sharing personal data through the flow.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform guests about what access-attempt data is collected and how it is used.

title: Guest code processing may lack a valid legal basis or exceed stated purpose
description: The Home Hub processes the guest's temporary access code and related access-attempt metadata. If this processing is retained, analyzed, or reused beyond the purpose of granting entry, or without appropriate notice and legal basis, the flow may violate data-protection obligations such as purpose limitation and data minimization.
assumptions: Assumes the code entry and related metadata qualify as personal data in context and that the system may store or reuse them.
uncertainty_note: Exact non-compliance node id is approximate because no specific Nc tree citation was provided in the retrieved context.

title: Excessive retention/disclosure of detailed sensor events in local log
description: The Home Hub writes motion, door, and other sensor events into the Local Event Log. Even though the storage is local, persisting fine-grained event histories can disclose occupants' presence, routines, sleep/work patterns, and absences to anyone with access to the log. If the full event stream is stored when only aggregated or short-lived records are needed, this is an avoidable data disclosure through over-collection/over-retention at the datastore.
assumptions: Sensor events are linkable to a household or identifiable occupants, and the log retains timestamped raw events beyond what is strictly necessary for the hub's function.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgment based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; the retrieved context did not provide a more specific Dd subtree for this exact case.

title: Identifiability of household members from timestamped event log
description: A local event log containing timestamped motion, door, and sensor events can make specific individuals or the household identifiable by revealing distinctive behavioral signatures, occupancy schedules, and device usage patterns. The datastore therefore creates a privacy threat if event granularity or retention enables singling out or association with known residents.
assumptions: The event log is associated with a specific home or account and contains timestamps/device identifiers sufficient to distinguish patterns of particular residents.
uncertainty_note: Specific subtree id is approximate; applicability of Identifiability is strong, but the exact node numbering may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Linkability of separate in-home activities through consolidated event logging
description: By writing multiple sensor events into one local log, the system enables linking events across rooms, devices, and times. Correlating door openings, motion detections, and other sensor triggers can reveal that separate observations belong to the same household context or person, allowing reconstruction of routines and sequences of behavior.
assumptions: The log stores common identifiers, timestamps, or device metadata that allow correlation across event types.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subtree id is best-judgment; the threat itself is well supported for consolidated event logs.

title: Detectability of occupancy and activities from presence of logged events
description: Even without reading full event contents, the existence, timing, frequency, or size of writes to the Local Event Log may make household activity detectable. Observers with access to the datastore or its metadata could infer when someone is home, asleep, entering, or leaving based on logging patterns alone.
assumptions: An attacker or unauthorized observer can observe log existence, timestamps, file growth, or record counts, even if content access is limited.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; detectability here is based mainly on metadata and write-pattern observation.

title: Logging of household sensor events without adequate consent or lawful basis
description: Recording detailed motion, door, and sensor events in a persistent local log may exceed what residents reasonably expect, especially for visitors or co-occupants who did not explicitly agree to such monitoring. If the hub logs these events without clear consent management, notice, or another valid legal basis, the flow creates a non-compliance threat.
assumptions: The deployment may involve multiple residents or visitors, and the system lacks explicit mechanisms to capture, communicate, or enforce consent/preferences for event logging.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, role of the operator, and product context; included because persistent in-home behavioral logging commonly raises consent/transparency obligations.

title: Upload metadata and account association can enable linkage of clips to a household
description: When the Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips to cloud storage, identifiers such as device ID, account ID, IP address, timestamps, and clip metadata can allow the cloud service or anyone with access to stored records to link multiple uploads to the same household and correlate activity over time.
assumptions: The upload includes persistent identifiers or metadata commonly needed for storage, synchronization, or account management.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed Linkability subtree.

title: Stored video clips reveal highly identifying household information
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded to cloud video storage may contain faces, voices, interiors, routines, visitors, and location cues. If stored without sufficient minimization or protection, the datastore enables identification of residents and visitors from the content itself or associated metadata.
assumptions: The clips contain personal data and are retained in a form accessible to the cloud provider or other authorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; retrieved context did not provide the Identifiability subtree.

title: Uploading full recorded clips may disclose more personal data than necessary
description: The Home Hub may upload entire recordings, including bystanders, private conversations, or periods irrelevant to the intended purpose, causing unnecessary disclosure of personal data to the cloud storage environment.
assumptions: No strong edge-side filtering, redaction, or event-based minimization is applied before upload.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; detailed Detectability/Disclosure subtree was not in retrieved context.

title: Presence and behavior patterns may be inferable from stored clip availability and metadata
description: Even without viewing clip contents, the existence, timing, size, and frequency of uploaded recordings in cloud storage can reveal when occupants are home, active, asleep, or away. This makes sensitive household behavior detectable from the datastore and its metadata.
assumptions: Clip metadata or object existence is observable to the provider, administrators, or an attacker with datastore access.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; retrieved context did not include the Detectability subtree.

title: Users and recorded individuals may be unaware that clips are uploaded to cloud storage
description: If the Home Hub uploads recordings automatically without clear notice or understandable settings, residents, guests, or passers-by may not realize that footage is transferred off-device and retained in the cloud, undermining transparency and awareness.
assumptions: The system may default to cloud backup or provide insufficient just-in-time notice about upload behavior.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; retrieved context did not include the Unawareness subtree.

title: Cloud storage may retain camera clips longer than necessary
description: Uploaded camera clips may be stored in cloud video storage beyond the period needed for the stated purpose, violating the storage limitation principle and increasing privacy risk for residents, visitors, and bystanders.
assumptions: Retention periods are undefined, overly long, or not enforced consistently in the cloud datastore.

title: Uploading raw clips to cloud storage may exceed data minimization and purpose limitation expectations
description: The Home Hub may transfer more personal data than necessary for the intended service purpose, for example full-resolution clips with audio and extensive metadata when a shorter excerpt, redacted version, or local-only storage would suffice. This can create non-compliance with data minimization or purpose limitation obligations.
assumptions: The service purpose could be achieved with less data or less intrusive processing.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement and may not exactly match the official detailed Non-compliance subtree.

title: Excessive disclosure in real-time motion alert payload
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than necessary in the motion alert to the backend, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, room/location labels, occupancy context, or raw sensor details, when a minimal event notification would suffice. This unnecessarily increases disclosure of in-home behavioral data across the process boundary.
assumptions: The motion alert contains or can be linked to household/person-related data, making it personal data. The backend does not strictly require all included fields for alert handling.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen as best judgement for explicit, avoidable disclosure/minimality on a process-to-process flow; retrieved context confirms Dd applicability but does not provide the exact subtree node text.

title: Stable identifiers in alerts enable linking of motion events over time
description: If the Home Hub includes persistent hub, household, sensor, or user identifiers in each real-time motion alert, the backend can trivially correlate alerts across time and reconstruct occupancy and activity patterns for the same home. This creates a linking risk beyond the immediate purpose of delivering a single alert.
assumptions: Alerts carry stable identifiers or metadata that remain constant across events and permit correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is best-effort; applicability is based on repeated event correlation via persistent identifiers.

title: Motion alert content may identify a household or individual
description: Even without explicit names, the combination of hub identifiers, account references, address-linked device metadata, and event timing in the alert may allow the backend to identify a specific household or infer the identity of occupants. Real-time in-home motion data is often strongly identifying when tied to an account.
assumptions: The backend can associate the alert with an account, installation, or other identifying records.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is best-effort; threat is grounded in identifiability of account-linked smart-home telemetry.

title: Backend can infer sensitive occupancy and behavior patterns from alerts
description: By receiving real-time motion alerts, the mobile app backend can infer when occupants are home, awake, moving between rooms, or following routines. Over time this supports profiling of daily habits and presence/absence patterns, which exceeds the immediate semantics of a single motion event.
assumptions: The backend stores, aggregates, or can observe repeated alerts over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement for inference from observed event data; retrieved context only establishes D applicability at this flow.

title: Secondary use of motion alerts beyond alert delivery
description: The backend may process incoming motion alerts for analytics, product improvement, security scoring, advertising-related segmentation, or model training beyond the user's expected purpose of delivering a real-time notification. Such repurposing would constitute use of personal data beyond the original purpose.
assumptions: Backend operators have technical ability or business incentive to reuse alert data for additional purposes.
uncertainty_note: Purpose limitation concern is plausible for backend telemetry processing, but no explicit evidence of such secondary use is provided in the flow description.

title: Insufficient transparency or legal basis for transmitting motion alerts to backend
description: Sending real-time in-home motion events from the Home Hub to the backend may lack adequate notice, valid legal basis, or user control if users are not clearly informed that occupancy-related data leaves the local hub and is processed centrally. This creates a non-compliance risk around transparency, purpose limitation, and data minimization obligations.
assumptions: The system is subject to privacy/data-protection obligations and users may expect motion processing to remain local unless clearly disclosed.
uncertainty_note: Exact legal/compliance subtree node is best-effort; applicability depends on jurisdiction and actual notices/consent mechanisms.

title: Lack of evidence about user authorization for forwarding motion alerts
description: If the Home Hub forwards motion alerts without recording or conveying evidence that the user enabled cloud forwarding or alerting, the system may be unable to demonstrate that this privacy-relevant transmission was authorized or expected. This weakens accountability for the disclosure of in-home activity data.
assumptions: Cloud forwarding of motion alerts is configurable or consent/authorization-dependent.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation in LINDDUN is less commonly central for this kind of flow; included only because authorization/accountability for forwarding may matter if user choice exists.

title: Excessive detail in motion notification discloses personal data
description: The backend may include more personal data than necessary in the push notification payload or visible notification text, such as exact timestamps, camera snapshots, room/location labels, device identifiers, or occupancy inferences. Because notifications are delivered across platform push infrastructure and may be visible on the phone lock screen, this can disclose personal data beyond what is required to alert the homeowner.
assumptions: The notification contains or could contain personal/contextual details beyond a minimal alert, and the homeowner's phone may display notification content on the lock screen or route it via third-party push services.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement for avoidable explicit disclosure/minimisation on a Process->ExternalEntity flow; exact node label may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Notification content enables identification of the household or resident
description: If the pushed notification contains names, address fragments, camera/location labels, account identifiers, or other unique references, the recipient device or intermediaries could directly identify the homeowner or household. Even seemingly routine motion alerts can identify a specific residence when combined with account or device metadata.
assumptions: Notification payload or metadata includes identifiers tied to a specific user, household, or property.
uncertainty_note: Identification is plausible here, but depends on actual notification fields and metadata exposed to the device or push provider; tree node is approximate.

title: Motion alerts reveal presence and behavior patterns
description: A stream of motion-detected notifications can reveal when people are at home, moving around, sleeping, away, or following routines. Even without explicit identifiers, repeated alerts and their timing allow inference of household activities and occupancy patterns from the data sent to the homeowner's phone.
assumptions: Notifications are sent with timestamps/frequency sufficient to infer routines or occupancy.
uncertainty_note: Inference risk is strong for motion-event notifications, though exact granularity depends on notification frequency and content; tree node is approximate.

title: Notification purpose may be unclear or exceed user expectations
description: The homeowner may understand the notification as a simple alert, while the payload also conveys or exposes additional personal data such as detailed event context, derived occupancy information, or metadata shared through mobile push ecosystems. If the scope and purpose of this disclosure are not transparent, the user may be unaware of how their data is being used and exposed.
assumptions: The system does not clearly explain what data is included in notifications, why it is included, and what third parties may process it during delivery.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness depends on the product's notice/UX and privacy communications; tree node is approximate.

title: Pushing motion notifications may be non-compliant without proper legal basis and controls
description: Sending motion-event notifications can involve processing and disclosure of personal data, potentially including behavioral inferences and transfer via third-party push providers. If the system lacks valid consent or another legal basis, adequate transparency, configurable notification settings, retention limits, or data-minimisation controls, this flow may violate privacy obligations.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires a legal basis, transparency, minimisation, and user controls for this type of notification processing.
uncertainty_note: Compliance assessment is jurisdiction- and implementation-specific; included because this flow clearly processes potentially sensitive household-behavior data.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's disclosure to the cloud analytics vendor may still contain stable device, account, cohort, timestamp, or event-pattern attributes that allow records to be linked to the same user/device over time or correlated with other datasets held by the vendor.
assumptions: Aggregation is imperfect or includes persistent identifiers, fine-grained timestamps, small cohorts, or quasi-identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types but not detailed node ids for this specific case.

title: Analytics recipient may infer identities from aggregated usage data
description: The cloud analytics vendor may be able to identify a user, household, or device behind supposedly aggregated analytics by combining the received data with auxiliary information, prior submissions, IP/account context, or other customer datasets.
assumptions: Vendor has access to auxiliary datasets or the aggregation granularity is insufficient to prevent singling out.
uncertainty_note: Applies if aggregation is weak or cohorts are small; if the data is strongly anonymized this threat may not materialize.

title: Received analytics can disclose sensitive behavior patterns
description: Even without direct identifiers, device-usage analytics can reveal private habits, routines, app usage patterns, location/timezone inferences, sleep/work cycles, or other sensitive behavioral information once processed by the analytics vendor.
assumptions: Usage metrics include sufficiently granular temporal, feature, or cohort information to reveal behavior.
uncertainty_note: Exact sensitivity depends on the analytics schema, which is not provided.

title: Vendor may be unaware of user consent limits or downstream restrictions
description: If the backend shares analytics without conveying the precise consent status, purpose limitation, retention limits, or contractual restrictions attached to the data, the analytics vendor may process it under incorrect assumptions, causing users to lose awareness and control over how their data is handled.
assumptions: Consent/preferences and usage restrictions are not fully propagated with the shared dataset.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk in third-party analytics sharing, but the flow description does not explicitly state whether consent metadata accompanies the data.

title: Secondary use by analytics vendor may exceed the original purpose
description: The cloud analytics vendor could use the received analytics for purposes beyond supporting the mobile app's analytics function, such as service improvement, benchmarking, model training, profiling, or combining with other customers' data, making the processing unexpected from the user's perspective.
assumptions: Contractual or technical controls do not strictly limit the vendor's purposes.
uncertainty_note: Depends on the vendor agreement and technical segregation controls, which are not described.

title: Sharing analytics with a third-party vendor may lack a valid legal basis or exceed data-minimization limits
description: Sending device-usage analytics to an external analytics vendor can violate privacy obligations if the backend shares more data than necessary, lacks valid consent or another legal basis, transfers data across jurisdictions improperly, or fails to honor opt-out/preferences.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires consent, minimization, transparency, transfer safeguards, or processor controls for third-party analytics sharing.
uncertainty_note: Specific compliance outcome depends on jurisdiction, contracts, and whether the analytics are truly anonymized.

title: Backend retrieval of stored video can reveal homeowner activity patterns
description: When P2 retrieves a stored video clip from DS2, the clip content and associated metadata (timestamps, camera/location identifiers, event labels) can allow the backend to learn or expose sensitive information about the homeowner's presence, routines, visitors, and behavior. This is a genuine linkability/disclosure risk at the receiving process because the retrieval action makes previously stored observations available for further processing.
assumptions: P2 can access the clip content and/or metadata in identifiable form and is not strictly limited to transient pass-through handling.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types/positions but not the detailed subtree for this exact case.

title: Retrieved clip can identify the homeowner or other individuals
description: The video clip retrieved by P2 may contain faces, voices, home interiors, device identifiers, or account-linked metadata that directly or indirectly identify the homeowner, household members, or visitors. The privacy threat is located at P2 because the receiving process obtains data that can be used to identify natural persons.
assumptions: Stored clips are associated with a user account or contain recognizable personal data.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is inferred from general LINDDUN Pro identification threats rather than explicitly provided in the retrieved snippets.

title: Backend retrieval may exceed what is necessary for playback
description: To serve playback, P2 may retrieve more personal data than needed, such as full-resolution video, extended retention metadata, unrelated event context, or additional clips. Receiving and processing excessive data at P2 creates a detectability/disclosure-style privacy risk because unnecessary personal information becomes available beyond the minimum needed for the homeowner's request.
assumptions: The implementation may fetch full objects or extra metadata rather than a minimized subset strictly required for playback.
uncertainty_note: This is a minimization-oriented interpretation of LINDDUN's disclosure/detectability family; applicability depends on implementation details not provided.

title: Playback retrieval can expose highly sensitive household information
description: A stored home-security video clip may reveal special-category or otherwise highly sensitive information, such as health conditions, religious practices, intimate situations, children, or inside-the-home activities. By retrieving the clip, P2 handles data whose sensitivity can cause significant privacy harm if improperly accessed, logged, cached, or reused.
assumptions: Clips may depict inside-home scenes or other sensitive contexts, not merely low-sensitivity outdoor footage.
uncertainty_note: Detailed Dd subtree node is best-effort; the sensitivity rationale is strong but depends on the nature of the recorded footage.

title: Secondary use of retrieved video beyond playback may be insufficiently controlled
description: Once P2 retrieves the stored clip for playback, the same data could also be used for analytics, model training, employee troubleshooting, law-enforcement response workflows, or product improvement without being necessary for the homeowner's immediate playback purpose. This creates an unawareness risk if users are not clearly informed about such downstream uses.
assumptions: P2 or connected services may retain, inspect, or repurpose retrieved clips or metadata beyond transient delivery.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on whether any secondary processing occurs; the flow description alone does not confirm it.

title: Retrieval and handling of stored clips may not align with consent or user expectations
description: The homeowner may expect the backend to retrieve the clip solely to fulfill the playback request. If P2 retrieves, caches, logs, or otherwise processes the clip in ways not covered by the user's consent, contract terms, or regional privacy requirements, the flow can contribute to non-compliance. The threat is located at P2 because compliance obligations attach to how the receiving process handles the personal data upon retrieval.
assumptions: Applicable obligations require purpose limitation, transparency, minimization, and lawful basis for any processing beyond requested playback.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual legal basis, notices, and controls, which are not provided.
